fields.v: Zhu, H., Zhang, Q., Wang, J., Yang, Z., Qiu, Y. (2026). Needle in the Repo: Diagnosing Maintainability Failures in AI-Generated Repository Edits. In: Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26), Munich, Germany, October 12-16, 2026. ACM, pp. 892-903. https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3834401
Conference — ASE '26 (41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering), Munich, ACM, DOI 10.1145/3832783.3834401
Qualcomm, Santa Clara, USA (Zhu; research conducted before joining Qualcomm); University of California, Riverside, USA (Zhang, Yang, Qiu); Tulane University, New Orleans, USA (Wang)

Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — Needle in the Repo (NITR), a probe-and-oracle framework of 21 C++ repository probes over 9 maintainability dimensions with hidden functional tests and structural oracles, used to evaluate 23 coding configurations (11 agent-mode, 12 API-only) of GPT, Claude, Gemini and Qwen models and to compare agent vs API modes

No SDD approach. Configurations: agent mode through 'provider-managed CLI surfaces' (CLI tools and versions not named) and API-only through Google Vertex AI (Qwen, Gemini, Claude) and the OpenAI API. Models: GPT-5.3-Cx, GPT-5.2-Cx, GPT-5, GPT-5.4, GPT-5-Mini, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Qwen3-Coder, Qwen3-80B

N/A (no approach). Each probe: starter code, agent-visible TASK.md (natural engineering request that does not reveal the dimension or oracle), author-facing SPEC.md (hidden), hidden evaluator (functional tests + structural oracle); multi-step probes give TASK1-TASK3.md in sequence

Probe construction: repository scenario selection → starter-code shaping → agent-facing task design → micro vs multi-step. Evaluation: temporary workspace, model edits applied (JSON map of file contents), CMake build, hidden functional tests, structural oracles; multi-step steps applied to the code of the previous step
None during runs. Oracles validated by the authors during construction against intended, shortcut and near-miss variants; failed runs inspected manually afterwards
N/A (no SDD approach); single edits (micro) and sequential edits (multi-step); agent mode restricted to read-only repository access, no command execution or external tools
Not classifiable (no SDD; authors do not use SDD terms; the task is a natural-language TASK.md and the SPEC.md is hidden from the agent)
Existing code base (edits to small authored multi-file C++ starter repositories)
21 probes (10 micro, 11 multi-step) over 9 dimensions (2-3 probes each); 483 (configuration, case) outcomes; repository size in LOC not stated
Small authored C++ repositories (e.g., multi-type add utility, filter pipeline, pricing extension, CV pipeline, cache lifecycle, session expiry, logging); no application domain
N/A (no human participants)
None

Hidden functional tests per probe; pass rate where a probe passes only if functional tests and structural oracle both succeed; outcome categories Pass, F (functional failure), S (tests pass, oracle fails), B (both fail), E (build error)

Probe-specific structural oracles for 9 maintainability dimensions (D1 change locality, D2 reuse and repo awareness, D3 responsibility decomposition, D4 extension structure, D5 interface and substitutability, D6 dependency control, D7 testability and determinism, D8 state ownership and lifecycle, D9 side-effect isolation); per-dimension pass rates; share of S outcomes
None
Failure archetypes from manual inspection (shortcut over reuse or abstraction, boundary contamination, incomplete abstraction refactor, later-step regression, missing test seam)

Automatic: local Python harness (workspace, apply edits, CMake build, hidden tests, Python structural oracles). Manual: qualitative inspection of the 308 failed runs (no coding protocol or agreement reported). One sampled run per configuration and case

Success criterion for all: a probe passes only if functional tests and structural oracle both pass; no threshold for 'works'. Values = cases passed of 21 (Table 3). Agent mode, CLI not named: (1) GPT-5.3-Cx 12 (57%); (2) GPT-5.2-Cx 11 (52%); (3) GPT-5 11 (52%); (4) GPT-5.4 10 (48%); (5) Claude Opus 4.6 12 (57%); (6) Claude Opus 4.5 10 (48%); (7) Claude Sonnet 4.6 9 (43%); (8) Claude Sonnet 4.5 8 (38%); (9) Gemini 3.1 Pro 10 (48%); (10) Gemini 3.1 Flash 6 (29%); (11) Gemini 2.5 Pro 5 (24%). API only: (12) GPT-5.4 7 (33%); (13) GPT-5-Mini 6 (29%); (14) GPT-5.3-Cx 6 (29%); (15) Claude Opus 4.5 6 (29%); (16) Claude Opus 4.6 6 (29%); (17) Claude Sonnet 4.5 6 (29%); (18) Claude Sonnet 4.6 5 (24%); (19) Gemini 3.1 Pro 8 (38%); (20) Gemini 2.5 Pro 6 (29%); (21) Gemini 3.1 Flash 5 (24%); (22) Qwen3-Coder 5 (24%); (23) Qwen3-80B 5 (24%). Quality verdict for each: no criterion stated by the authors. Cost verdict: not measured

Tasks: 21 probes. Configurations: 23 (11 agent-mode, 12 API-only); matched comparison for the 9 model families run in both modes; no other baseline. Held constant: TASK.md only, no hints or maintainability instructions, JSON output format, hidden tests and oracles. Differences: agent mode sees its prior edits in multi-step cases and has read-only repository access; API receives each step independently with prior context. Acceptance: hidden functional tests + structural oracles. Repetitions: single sampled run per case. Human intervention: none

Pass rates 24%-57%, average 36.2%; best GPT-5.3-Cx (Agt) and Claude Opus 4.6 (Agt) 12/21, best API Gemini 3.1 Pro 8/21; five probes unsolved by all. Micro 53.5% (123/230) vs multi-step 20.6% (52/253); API 44.2% → 13.6%, agent 63.6% → 28.1%. Dimensions: D6 4.3%, D3 15.2%, D5 26.1%, D2 31.9%, D4 41% (Table 3 bottom row only), D7 44.9%, D1 47.8%, D9 47.8%, D8 58.7%. Outcomes: 36.2% pass, 31.5% F, 13.3% S (64/483), 10.4% B, 8.7% E. Agent mode 45.0% vs API 28.2% (+16.8 pp), better in 8 of 9 matched families (average +3.0 cases); authors call it observational, not causal. No significance tests

Distinguished configurations (24%-57%) and dimensions, and exposed 64 behaviourally correct but structurally failing outcomes missed by tests. Not repeated: single run per case, no variance or prompt-sensitivity estimate. Limitations stated: agent and API settings differ in interface, so harness-level comparison only; 2-3 cases per dimension give diagnostic trends, not high-power estimates; oracles are lightweight targeted checks

Threats: construct (maintainability as authored probes and case-specific oracles, not maintainability in general), internal (harness-level comparisons; single run; no prompt sensitivity), external (21 small C++ repositories; other languages, scales and workflows not covered), conclusion (few cases per dimension). Gaps / implications: treat AI-generated multi-step changes as structurally untrusted proposals; review beyond test passing; agents need repository-level structural reasoning; make maintainability a first-class evaluation objective

Inconsistencies: Table 2 S row gives 13 S outcomes for Case 001, 0 for Case 002 and 11 for Case 020 (32 in total) (p. 898), while the text gives 17/23, 16/23 and 15/23 and 64 in total (pp. 895, 898-899); a count of Fig. 6 gives 17 S for Case 001, matching the text. Table 3 Agent avg. 9.5 vs text 9.45 (rounding). Agent CLI tools not named ('Cx' not expanded). Artifact: https://github.com/ucrriple/NITR and Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21154293. Pre-registration: not claimed. Programming language: C++ (CMake); oracles and harness in Python

fields.why: Authors are academic and not vendors of the evaluated models, but the acknowledgements list 'Google Research Credit Awards' among the funding, and Gemini models (Google) are evaluated. Funding is not authorship, so Yes is defensible; a stricter reader could give Partly.
fields.doubt: Os agradecimentos referem 'Google Research Credit Awards' e o estudo avalia modelos Gemini da Google. Decide se este financiamento (créditos) afeta a independência: Yes ou Partly.
